# General Review Lessons

- Make a guard's zero-match check count only the matches it is meant to protect. Matches that are always present, like the guard's own allowed cases, keep the check from ever firing.
- Test a guard by planting a violation and by breaking its detection, and see it fail both times. A guard that passes on clean code proves nothing.
- Before acting on a review finding, check whether existing tests or contracts explain the current shape. A structural test can be why the code looks the way it does.
- When code reads a user-owned config into a typed struct and writes it back, keep the fields it does not model. Any new reason to rewrite the file otherwise silently deletes user data.
- Make a new outer timeout longer than every internal budget on that path. Otherwise the kill fires before the code's own graceful fallback.
- Before setting an explicit timeout, look up the platform's current default for that exact event; an explicit value can shorten the budget rather than add one.
- When splitting known from unknown JSON keys to preserve them, decode only the exact known keys and keep every other key, case variants included, as unknown. `encoding/json` matches field names case-insensitively, so decoding the whole object lets a key like `"Command"` overwrite the real field.
- When a change makes a fix command riskier, changes which command to run, or adds a new place that reports an existing failure, check every place that already reports it (status, doctor, enable, help text) so they all give the same fix. Otherwise one screen sends people to the safe fix and the next to the destructive one, or one command prints the same failure twice with different fixes.
- When a test plants a failure to cover an error branch, make sure an earlier step doesn't fail first; otherwise the assertion passes without ever running that branch.
- Select an agent's final report by a marker it carries (such as the contract line), not by its position in the event stream; a trailing tool call or an empty message ID moves a position-based boundary.
- When code keeps state so a later run can retry, test the retry itself. A test that checks the kept state against the same expression the code uses would pass even if that expression were wrong.
- When decoding user-editable JSON into maps or pointers, skip null elements before writing to them; `[null]` decodes to a nil map and a write panics.
- Review a PR that is behind main against current main, not its own base: build both and run the same repro. Its tests pass on its old base even when keeping its side of a conflict would undo a fix merged since.
- When wiring user config into a new path, test it with a broken config too. A user rule that silently fails to load leaks the same way as one that was never wired.
- Make a fail-closed check fire only on the failure it guards against, not on a whole class of errors. A refusal on any settings error blocks unrelated cases and pushes users toward a less safe escape hatch, such as an unredacted `--raw` bundle.
- Read the Trail's current description and resolved findings before drafting review comments. The trail description can be newer than the PR description and may already list known follow-ups, which turns "you missed this" into a question about scale or timing.
- When a PR claims corpus validation, check what the corpus contained, and test on inputs from outside it, such as other languages and other codebases. A corpus drawn from one codebase can pass while common idioms elsewhere break.

with its reason. Facts about a single repo stay in that repo's memory.

  or in a repo's memory. I want to approve anything persisted on my behalf.
- In code comments, state only what you verified. Check claims about external

  constant instead of copying its value. A wrong default in a comment once hid

  diff, and offer it as an option, not a requirement.
- On public threads, write in lowercase, first person, casual but precise, and
  never blame anyone. Keep review comments soft: frame points as questions or

Closes #2378

Related to #2350 and #2358.

Entire keeps uncondensed checkpoint commits reachable through shadow branches. Cleanup could mistake incomplete safety evidence for proof that a branch was unused: expired state with pending work could be removed, a ref read failure could be treated as absence, and malformed records could be omitted from cleanup inventory. Each path could leave shadow-only checkpoint history unreachable.

## Why cleanup could orphan history

Session state older than seven days was purged based on age even when it still recorded uncondensed checkpoint work. Separately, go-git can report an unreadable loose ref as not found, and session discovery treated that result as proof that the ref was absent. Once either state record disappeared, later cleanup saw no session protecting the shadow branch.

The cleanup inventory was also tolerant by default, so an unreadable state record could disappear from the evidence used to authorize deletion. Finally, the last protection check happened before a separate ref-deletion operation, leaving a state-change window between check and deletion.

## Make destructive decisions fail closed

State expiration now preserves records that still carry pending checkpoint content. Reference absence must be positively established; ambiguous ref errors preserve the associated state.

Ordinary session discovery remains tolerant: it logs and skips an unreadable unrelated state instead of blocking healthy session linking. Destructive paths use a strict inventory so omitted state cannot authorize deletion.

Post-push cleanup now performs its final protection check inside a prepared native Git compare-and-swap transaction. Git holds the ref lock while the guard runs, and any uncertain or failed safety check aborts before the deletion commits. Doctor and reset cleanup use the same strict-inventory boundary.

The deliberate trade-off is that uncertainty may retain stale state or a shadow branch. That is preferable to making uncondensed checkpoint history unreachable.

## Verification

`mise run check` passed on the final tree, including:

- formatting and lint
- race-enabled unit and integration tests
- 56 Vogon canaries
- 4 Roger-Roger canaries

Regression coverage includes expired uncondensed sessions, unreadable refs, malformed session state, tolerant commit linking, and guarded ref deletion on files and reftable storage.

## Summary

Agent turns no longer write anything to git. Older versions committed a full working-tree snapshot to a per-worktree shadow branch (`entire/<commit>-<worktree>`) at every turn end. That was the source of runaway local storage, and cleaning those branches up at the wrong moment made uncondensed work unreachable. Turn ends now record pending work in session state only: the step count, the files the agent touched, and each touched file's git blob hash. A checkpoint is written only when you commit.

Line attribution is removed entirely, including the AI/Human/Mixed labels in `entire blame`, which now reports whether each line's commit is linked to a checkpoint. Checkpoint metadata no longer carries `initial_attribution` or `combined_attribution`; entire.io derives the experts counts from those and must be told they stop arriving.

Commits link to a session by file name: any committed path the session touched links it, except a new file at a path the agent deleted. Carry-forward after a partial commit compares the recorded hashes with the commit and the worktree, so a `git add -p` remainder, a pending deletion, or a session upgraded from the old state format keeps its uncommitted work. Gitignored files, submodule pointers, and paths inside a submodule or beneath a symlinked directory never enter the tracked files, so they can no longer keep a session pending forever; edits inside a submodule belong to the nested repository's own session. Whether a committed file still has uncommitted agent changes is asked of `git status`, so repositories with `text=auto` or `core.autocrlf` no longer keep fully committed files pending.

Lifecycle decisions (condensation, the zombie sweep, orphan cleanup, doctor) key on one predicate over session state instead of whether a shadow ref exists. Pending step rows, explain of temporary checkpoints, incremental task checkpoints and the Claude Code post-todo hook install are gone. `checkpoint list --pending` now previews what the next commit's checkpoint will contain.

Claude Code gains a transcript prompt extractor, so its prompts no longer depend on `prompt.txt` alone.

Addresses #2663, #2378, #2350, #1730, #1807 and #2653. Supersedes trail 1486 (`soph/fix-shadow-after-midturn-commit`), which patches code this PR deletes.

## Migrations

Turn ends no longer write shadow branches (entire/<commit>-<worktree>): pending work is tracked in session state and checkpoints are written only when you commit. Branches left by older versions are not removed automatically. `entire doctor` and `entire status` report them, and `entire doctor --force` or `entire disable --uninstall` deletes the `entire/<commit>-<worktree>` form without touching session state. The oldest bare `entire/<commit>` form is only ever listed, since a branch of your own named after a short SHA looks the same; `entire clean --all` removes it behind a confirmation. Do not use plain `entire clean` for this: it also clears pending session state. They hold full snapshots of your working tree, so run it once after upgrading. Deleting the branches frees no space by itself: a later `git gc` reclaims it once their objects are two weeks old. `git gc --prune=now` frees it immediately, but it drops every unreachable object in the repository (recently dropped stashes included) and must only run when no other git process is active.

`entire blame --json` reports a per-line `status` (`checkpoint`, `commit`, `uncommitted`) instead of `authorship` and `tag`. Its summary reports checkpoint-linked, commit and uncommitted line counts instead of AI/Human/Mixed counts.

New checkpoints no longer include `initial_attribution`, `combined_attribution` or `prompt_attributions`; checkpoints written by older versions keep theirs, and rewrites (explain `--generate`, attach) carry them through unchanged. Session state files written by older versions still load; their attribution and `last_checkpoint_commit_hash` keys are dropped on the next save.

The Claude Code post-todo hook is no longer installed, and any `entire enable` prunes it and says so. Its subcommand stays so older hook configs keep working. An older CLI run against the same tracked `.claude/settings.json` reports the hooks as out of date and re-adds it; this CLI removes it again on the next `entire enable`.

`entire session info --json` and `entire session current --json` report the number of turns not yet condensed into a checkpoint as `pending_turns`. Cleanup can make uncondensed checkpoint commits unreachable after state expiry or a ref read failure
OPEN  
## What happened?

Entire keeps uncondensed checkpoint commits reachable through shadow branches. Cleanup uses session state to decide whether a shadow branch still contains work that must be preserved.

Two independent bugs can delete valid session state before condensation finishes:

1. Loading session state deletes it once it is more than seven days old, even when it records pending checkpoint work.
2. Session discovery deletes state when a Git ref lookup returns `plumbing.ErrReferenceNotFound`, even when the ref exists but could not be read.

Both bugs produce the same failure:

1. A session has checkpoint commits that exist only on its shadow branch.
2. Entire deletes the session state that associates those commits with pending work.
3. Cleanup classifies the shadow branch as unused and deletes it.
4. The shadow-only commits become unreachable.
5. Git may eventually garbage-collect them.

This affects checkpoint history that has not yet been condensed. It does not delete working-tree files or commits already reachable from ordinary Git branches.

### Bug 1: state expiry ignores pending work

`StateStore.Load` deletes session state after seven days based only on its timestamp.

It does not check whether the state still records uncondensed work. A valid state with `FullyCondensed: false` and a non-zero `StepCount` is therefore deleted as soon as it crosses the expiry threshold.

The expiry check is destructive. Merely loading the state removes the evidence cleanup needs to protect the corresponding shadow branch.

This affects both active and ended sessions.

### Bug 2: a ref read failure is treated as proof that the ref is absent

Session discovery removes state that appears to refer to a missing shadow branch.

An existing loose ref can be unreadable because of a filesystem error or permission problem. In that case, go-git may return `plumbing.ErrReferenceNotFound`. Session discovery treats that result as proof that the ref does not exist and deletes the state as orphaned.

If the ref becomes readable again, its session state is already gone. The next cleanup pass sees no session protecting the branch and deletes it.

A failed lookup is not enough evidence that deleting the state is safe.

## Steps to reproduce

### State expiry

1. Create a shadow branch containing a commit that is not reachable from any ordinary branch.
2. Save valid session state for the shadow branch with `FullyCondensed: false` and `StepCount: 1`.
3. Set the session timestamps to one hour ago.
4. Run pushed-shadow cleanup.
5. Confirm that cleanup preserves the shadow branch.
6. Change only the timestamps so the state is eight days old.
7. Load the state or run the cleanup path that loads it.
8. Observe that Entire deletes both the state and the shadow branch.
9. Run `git fsck --unreachable --no-reflogs`.
10. Observe that the shadow-only commit is unreachable.

**Symptom.** A session is re-initialised from scratch every few turns: transcript window, owner, and home reset, and a commit landing in the gap finds no session at all. In one clone a single session was re-initialised 37 times in four days.

**Cause.** The strategy's session listing, which every hook runs to match sessions, deletes any non-active state whose shadow branch is gone and whose checkpoint ID is empty. Unfinalized IDLE states are never deleted by the listing: a live idle session stays, and a dead-owner one is left for `finalizeExitedSessions`, which marks it ENDED so the next listing clears it. ### Turn-End State

A turn end (`SaveStep`) writes no git objects. It records the turn into session state and leaves the transcript on local disk:

- `StepCount` is incremented, `FilesTouched` gains the turn's modified, new and deleted paths, and `TouchedFileHashes` records the git blob hash of each modified or new regular file (hashed with `git hash-object`, so clean filters apply exactly as `git add` would) and `""` for each deleted path. A path whose hash is unknown — hashing failed, a symlink, or a path that arrived through a task record, a per-tool hook, or a Codex child-file merge (`MergeUnhashedFilesTouched`, which also drops any hash an earlier step recorded for it) — has no entry and falls back to name matching. content.text:
I reviewed [entireio/cli#2385](https://github.com/entireio/cli/pull/2385) without changing anything. Most of the published PR is obsolete: upstream [entireio/cli#2692](https://github.com/entireio/cli/pull/2692), merged Oct 8, removed shadow branches. Your uncommitted work cuts the PR to a 3-file fix, which builds and passes its tests on current main. Notes for the sibling sessions are in `pr-2385-fix-session-cleanup-safety.md` in the shared notes folder.

## 1. Local worktree vs the published PR

- **Published head** is `c164844c2` (Sep 17): 19 files, +747/−154. GitHub says it **conflicts** with main.
- **Local-only commit (not pushed):** one merge, `7b6f9c225` "Merge upstream/main" (Oct 14). It took upstream's side for every shadow-branch path. That left dead code behind with no production callers: `ListStrict`, `ListSessionStatesStrict`, `CompareAndSwapRefGuarded`, `ReferenceIsAbsent` and `HasShadowBranchContent`.
- **Staged changes:** they put 7 files back exactly as main has them, which deletes that dead code.
- **Unstaged changes:** the PR shrinks to 3 files.
  - In `StateStore.load`, an expired session is deleted only if `!HasPendingWork()` ([state.go:1246](cmd/entire/cli/session/state.go:1246)).
  - A 45-line retention test.
  - The stale-delete test fixture no longer sets `StepCount`.
- On top of current main (`a334cb698`) this merges and applies cleanly. Build, vet, the session and gitrepo packages, and the stale/orphan/sweep strategy tests all pass. The one failure was `TestNewStateStore_RefusesRealRepoUnderGoTest`, and only because my scratch copy isn't a git repo.

## 2. Brief

**What it does for users:** today Entire deletes any session state file that has been idle for 7 days, even when it holds agent work that hasn't been checkpointed yet. Come back after a week, commit the agent's files, and the commit no longer links to a checkpoint. The local change keeps those files.

**Why it still matters:** the published PR guarded shadow-branch deletion, and #2692 deleted that code. #2692 also lists #2378, this PR's issue, as addressed, but #2378 is still open. Now that turn ends write nothing to git, the state file is the *only* record of pending work. Main's own comment on `OwnerExited` admits that the 7-day purge discards "pending checkpoint work instead of condensing it".

**Performance, compatibility, data:** no format change, and the cost is negligible. The risk is that some state files are now kept with no end date (see findings 1 and 2).

**Uncertain:** whether maintainers accept retention with no end date. #2573 says deletion belongs to "the sweeper, doctor and the 7-day expiry", and #617 treated sessions that never expire as a bug.

## Findings (on the local version)

1. **Medium: some sessions are now never deleted.** `HasPendingWork()` ignores `FullyCondensed`. A fully condensed, ended session that still has a task record is kept forever. Doctor skips it ([doctor.go:377-381](cmd/entire/cli/doctor.go:377)) and says that kind of record "can never complete". The sweep and orphan cleanup skip it too.
   - **Option:** delete an expired session when `FullyCondensed || !HasPendingWork()`.
2. **Medium: the sweep's 7-day limit disappears.** The docs say the 7-day purge bounds the zombie sweep ([sessions-and-checkpoints.md:277](docs/architecture/sessions-and-checkpoints.md:277)). A session that keeps failing to condense would now start a background sweep every 15 minutes with no end date.
   - **Needed:** keep a limit, or say why none is needed. Then update the `StaleSessionThreshold` doc comment ([state.go:30](cmd/entire/cli/session/state.go:30)), [manual_commit_session.go:164](cmd/entire/cli/strategy/manual_commit_session.go:164) and [checkpoint-implementation.md:66](docs/development/checkpoint-implementation.md:66).
3. **Medium: the test doesn't prove the fix.** It checks that the file survives, which just restates the condition in the code. Your General.md lesson ("test the retry itself") applies. An integration test should age a session with pending files, commit those files, and check that the commit still gets its checkpoint.
4. **Low:** the published version also kept sessions with `TurnCheckpointIDs` or `CondensationAttempt` set. The local version drops both by switching to `HasPendingWork`. That matches upstream's single-check rule; say so in the PR.

Your cli.md lesson (the bare-repo/`GIT_DIR` check) doesn't apply here.

## 3. Review readiness

- **CI has never run.** All runs on all 4 pushes failed with 0 jobs ("workflow file issue"). Your other fork PRs hit the same thing Sep 7-18, and #2213 ran fine on Oct 14, so a new push should get real CI.
- **Reviews:** none, and no comments. It's waiting on cli-maintainers.
- **Mergeability:** conflicts in 8 files, one of them a file main deleted that this PR modifies.
- **Trail:** there is none on entireio/cli. The fork has trail [gh/MuskanPaliwal/cli#3](https://entire.io/gh/MuskanPaliwal/cli/trails/3), which isn't linked to the PR and is titled after #2350. Its 2 open medium findings both point at `cleanup.go` code upstream deleted, and both look wrong anyway.
- **PR body:** it describes code that no longer exists.

## Recommended next steps

1. Fix findings 1-3 on the local change. I'd give you a pre-edit brief first.
2. Commit the staged and unstaged work, and push to the existing PR to replace the published head.
3. Rewrite the PR title and description to cover only the stale-state fix.
4. Create a Trail on entireio/cli and link it.
5. Ask whether [entireio/cli#2378](https://github.com/entireio/cli/issues/2378) Bug 2 and [entireio/cli#2350](https://github.com/entireio/cli/issues/2350) can be closed as fixed by #2692.

The other option is to close #2385 in favour of a fresh, focused PR. I'll wait for your go-ahead either way.
